note: Dante fainted at the end of Canto 5. For the second time he wakes in a new circle, with no account of how he got there.
Francesca and Paolo. Dante's word is cognati, in-laws: a blunt reminder that he was her husband's brother.
The circle of the gluttons, the second of the sins of weak self-control.

quote: Massive hail and dark water and snow
note: The punishment answers the sin. Those who lived for fine food and drink, warm and comfortable at table, lie in stinking mud under a cold, filthy rain, like pigs in a sty.

context: Dante gives him a beard and clawed hands, half dog and half man: a picture of gluttony itself, with three mouths and a swollen belly. He doesn't only guard the souls, he torments them.

note: The sinners have come to resemble their keeper. Appetite has made them animals.
"Worm" was an old word for a dragon or any loathsome monster. Dante uses it again for Lucifer himself in Inferno 34.
In the Aeneid the Sibyl, Aeneas's guide, quiets Cerberus with a honey-cake laced with drugs. Dante's Virgil needs only dirt: blind appetite will swallow anything.

quote: what seemed like bodies but was only emptiness
context: The travelers walk straight over the gluttons, whose bodies offer no resistance to a living foot.

quote: You were created before I was destroyed
note: You were born before I died, so you must have known me. The Italian plays on two words: Dante was fatto, made, before the speaker was disfatto, unmade.

context: The first mention of Florence in the poem, and the first Florentine Dante meets. He speaks of it at once as a sack overflowing with envy.

note: Nothing certain is known of him. Ciacco may be a pet form of the name Giacomo, or a nickname: early commentators say the word meant "hog". Boccaccio, in the Decameron, tells a story about a Florentine glutton of this name who was witty and welcome at every rich man's table.

The damned can see the future, as Inferno 10 explains. The poem is set in 1300 but was written years later, so Dante can put into their mouths, as prophecy, things that had already happened. This is the first of the poem's political prophecies.

context: In the spring of 1300, when the poem is set, the two factions were on the edge of open violence, and Dante was about to take office in the city's government.

note: On May Day 1300, a few weeks after the date of the journey, young men of the two factions fought in the street and blood was drawn. Florentines counted the open feud from that day.
The Whites, Dante's own side. The name comes from their leaders, the Cerchi family, who had come into the city from the countryside. In 1301 they banished the leaders of the Blacks.
The Blacks came back in November 1301 and seized the city. In 1302 they banished the leading Whites, and Dante, away from Florence at the time, was among those condemned. He never saw his city again.

quote: one who now waits on the sidelines
context: Almost all commentators take this to be Pope Boniface, who in 1300 seemed to favor neither side. In 1301 he sent the French prince Charles of Valois to Florence as a peacemaker, and Charles let the Blacks take the city. Dante's word suggests a ship hugging the coast, waiting to see which way to steer.

note: Nobody knows who they are. Some guess Dante himself and a friend. Others take "two" to mean simply very few, as in the biblical stories where a handful of just men can't save a city.
The three sins Dante blames for the ruin of Florence. Some readers match them with the three beasts of Canto 1.

context: Dante asks after the great Florentines of the generations before his own. He will meet Farinata in Inferno 10.

note: The only one of the five who is never mentioned again in the poem. Who he was is uncertain.

quote: who set their minds on doing good
note: Good in the public sense: they served their city well. The answer is a shock to Dante. Civic merit doesn't save a soul, and all of them are deeper in Hell than Ciacco.

quote: bring me back to others' memory
note: Many souls in the upper circles ask for this. To be remembered among the living is the only kind of survival left to them. At the bottom of Hell the traitors want the opposite: to be forgotten.
The trumpet that announces the Last Judgment at the end of time, when the dead rise (Matthew 24:31; 1 Corinthians 15:52).
Christ, coming to judge the living and the dead. He is hostile only to the damned.

quote: take back his flesh and human shape
note: The resurrection of the body. Christian teaching holds that at the Last Judgment every soul, saved or damned, will be joined to its body again and hear its sentence confirmed forever.

The philosophy of Aristotle, as Christian thinkers such as Thomas Aquinas taught it. A human being is soul and body together, so a soul with its body is more complete than a soul alone, and a more complete creature feels more. After the Judgment the damned will suffer more, and the blessed will rejoice more.

context: He guards the way down to the fourth circle, where sins of money are punished. "The great enemy" because wealth, for Dante, is the great enemy of human peace.
